items.title: ARISE: Adapting to Evolving Capability Gaps in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: ARISE addresses the challenge of evolving capability gaps in long-horizon reinforcement learning agents. Its core method, Adaptive Rubric-Skill Co-Evolution (ARISE), continuously adapts evaluation criteria and exploration strategies based on agent performance. This allows the agent to focus learning on emerging weaknesses and make progress even with sparse task-level feedback.

items.title: Continuous Context Management
items.abstract: This paper introduces Continuous Context Management (CCM) for LLM agents, which compacts interaction history at every turn instead of waiting for a threshold. This prevents the active prompt from growing excessively, significantly reducing input usage and prompt size. While CCM initially lowers task success for most models, it can be improved through fine-tuning with privileged distillation, demonstrating a novel approach to efficient long-horizon LLM agent operation.

items.title: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: This paper introduces KV-streams, a novel method to improve the efficiency of context compaction in agentic reinforcement learning. Instead of repeatedly refilling the LLM's context, KV-streams stream the KV cache forward, significantly boosting training throughput (2.6-5x speedup) without compromising performance. This approach also allows the streamed KV cache to act as a recurrent state, preserving long-term information.

items.title: SEABench: Benchmarking Endogenous Misalignment In Self-Evolving Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces SEABench, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate "endogenous misalignment" in self-evolving AI agents. The core method involves creating longitudinal task sequences in a personal assistant environment to observe how agents' self-modifications can lead to unsafe behavior over time, even without external adversarial input. SEABench's contribution is providing a standardized way to study this emerging risk and an adaptive pipeline to discover and attribute failures in these evolving systems.

items.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
items.abstract: TokenCast addresses the unpredictable token consumption of LLM agents by learning a composable cost representation for execution segments. This method estimates future token usage by accounting for both segment-specific consumption and the context growth introduced, allowing for dynamic, real-time forecast updates without additional LLM calls. Its core contribution is enabling accurate and efficient prediction of token costs during LLM agent execution.

items.title: Rethinking Personalized Generation: Test-Time Alignment via Factorized Ranking Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes a test-time alignment method for personalized generation with LLMs. It argues that personalization is a candidate matching problem, not a generator limitation, and that existing reward models are ill-suited for this. The core contribution is a parameter-efficient framework using small MLP ranking models that leverage base LLM embeddings to efficiently score and select personalized outputs.
items.figure_caption: Personalization headroom under Best-of- N N sampling. The oracle selects with the evaluation metric itself and upper-bounds any selector; the reward-model line is, at each N N , the best of the four generalist reward models of Section 4.1 . The shaded region is the gap between them. Results are averaged over the three datasets of each task.

items.title: ScAn-Bench: Evaluating Scaling Analysis Methodology
items.abstract: This paper introduces ScAn-Bench, a novel benchmark for evaluating methodologies used to derive scaling laws and optimal prescriptions for large foundation models. The authors systematically analyze data acquisition and extrapolation techniques across language and vision-language models, identifying a critical gap in current research. Their contribution lies in providing the first comprehensive evaluation of scaling analysis methodology, facilitating future advancements in model scaling.

items.title: AutoRef: Harness Optimization for Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation
items.abstract: This paper introduces AutoRef, a method to optimize the "harness" in agentic multi-reference image generation. AutoRef automatically tunes how reference images are processed and how generated outputs are evaluated to improve fidelity and naturalness. Its contribution lies in providing a systematic approach to enhance the complex decision-making process within these generative agents.

items.title: BaRe-Mem: Bayesian Reliability Memory for Robust and Adaptive Agent Consultation
items.abstract: BaRe-Mem is a Bayesian memory system that estimates advisor reliability in multi-agent systems by analyzing the central model's beliefs and past interactions. This allows it to dynamically adjust the influence of advisor responses and decide whether to consult or reason autonomously, making it more robust to misleading information than existing methods. Its contribution lies in providing a principled and adaptive approach to agent consultation and worker allocation, improving performance and reliability.

items.title: Behavioral Foundation Models for Quality Diversity
items.abstract: This paper introduces BFM-QD, a framework that leverages the latent space of Behavioral Foundation Models (BFMs) for Quality-Diversity (QD) search. Instead of searching in high-dimensional policy parameters, BFM-QD efficiently discovers diverse and high-performing behaviors within a compact latent space. A key contribution is a novel, critic-free policy improvement operator that approximates policy gradients without requiring backpropagation.

items.title: Distillation Defenses Easily Break After Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: This paper reveals that defenses against distillation attacks on large language models are often ineffective because they don't account for attackers further training their distilled models with reinforcement learning. This subsequent training significantly lowers the bar for attackers to steal advanced reasoning capabilities from closed-source models, undermining existing security measures.
items.figure_caption: A distillation attack’s pipeline. Attackers amass large volumes of reasoning traces from proprietary LLMs and train (“distill”) their own models on these traces, followed by further training of distilled models with reinforcement learning (RL). Existing threat models assume attackers train models only with distillation, while a realistic distillation attack likely follows distillation with RL.

items.title: FactorEngram: Factorized N-gram Memory with Basis-Level Gating for Language Models
items.abstract: FactorEngram introduces a novel memory mechanism for language models that factorizes n-gram representations into shared basis vectors. This allows for more efficient parameter sharing and contextual gating at the basis level, enabling models to selectively retrieve relevant components of memory for polysemous patterns, unlike previous monolithic approaches. Its core contribution lies in enabling finer-grained memory access and improved semantic understanding through this factorized and gated memory structure.
items.figure_caption: Overview of FactorEngram. Left: memory modules are residually inserted before the attention module at selected Transformer layers. Right: n-gram lookups retrieve coefficients that are concatenated and modulated by context-dependent basis-level gates. The shared dictionary participates in both gating and memory reconstruction. The reconstructed memory is projected, refined by a short causal convolution, and added to the backbone hidden state.

items.title: Failure-Transparent Agents: Benchmarking Post-Failure Reporting in Tool-Using Language Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces Failure-Transparent Agents (FTA), a benchmark designed to isolate and evaluate how tool-using language models report failures. FTA controls for external factors, allowing direct auditing of post-failure claims by fixing the observed failure and required evidence. The contribution lies in providing a controlled environment to measure and improve models' honesty and accuracy in reporting tool failures, leading to significant reductions in false success and fabricated details.
items.figure_caption: FTA under a fixed post-failure evidence state. (a) A visible tool failure may still be followed by an unsupported success claim. (b) FTA holds the failed trace fixed, varies the response policy, and scores the resulting response against evaluator-side evidence and safe-recovery references. (c) Across all six models and 3,600 human-annotated responses, pooled false success is 22.8% under baseline, 9.3% with transparency, and 0.8% with the evidence contract.

items.title: MechBench: Can AI Scientific Agents Discover Mechanisms Beyond Phenomenal Laws?
items.abstract: This paper introduces MechBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI scientific agents' ability to discover underlying mechanisms, not just observable laws. MechBench separates these capabilities by providing agents with observational data and context, then testing their understanding of internal scientific consequences through "mechanism probes." The benchmark's novel tasks are generated by mutating known mechanisms, pushing agents beyond memorization to true mechanistic discovery.
items.figure_caption: From phenomenal-law recovery to mechanistic discovery.

items.title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether different reasoning methods in LLMs share a common underlying mechanism. By training and comparing various models on a multi-hop reasoning task, they discover that models performing reasoning in latent space generalize better to out-of-distribution problems than those relying on explicit intermediate traces like Chain-of-Thought. Their key contribution is identifying a recurrent search algorithm in latent reasoning that enables this improved depth generalization.

items.title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science
items.abstract: This paper introduces AI Night-Scientist, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance LLM creativity in scientific ideation. It trains models to balance predictable "day science" with serendipitous "night science" by modeling creativity across action, process, and outcome. The core contribution is a method to generate more diverse and novel scientific proposals by teaching LLMs when and how to deviate from standard reasoning.
items.figure_caption: Given an input task, creativity can be injected into three different axes of reasoning: action, process , and outcome . Moreover, each level can be executed with varying degrees of creativity .

items.title: Representation Alignment as a Bottleneck in LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
items.abstract: This paper argues that the failure of LLMs in chemical retrosynthesis planning stems from forcing them to simultaneously handle chemical analysis and planning language structuring. Their core method decomposes retrosynthesis into distinct stages: molecule mapping, reaction mapping, and PDDL generation. This approach successfully overcomes the bottleneck, demonstrating that representation alignment, not model capacity, is the key challenge, and highlighting the need for representation-centric design in future AI systems.

items.title: RSI-Master: Structuring Experiments to Guide Autonomous Model Improvement
items.abstract: RSI-Master introduces a novel framework for autonomous AI model improvement by structuring experiments to prevent "hacking" and "strategy lock-in." It employs an "Experiment OS" for regularized actions and traceable records, alongside a "Reviewer-Guided Research Orchestration" system that dynamically organizes exploration through a research Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). This approach ensures both safe, focused experimentation and broad exploration of research directions.
items.figure_caption: Overview of RSI-Master . The Experiment OS defines permitted operations for data development, training, and evaluation and maintains persistent, linked experimental records. Reviewer-Guided Research Orchestration grows a DAG of research directions: Workers explore directions through experiments, Reviewers compare the resulting evidence, and the Main Agent uses their reviews to continue, verify, branch, or revise directions.

items.title: Share-Borne AI Virus: Memory-Hopping Attacks Across LLM Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces "artifact-mediated propagation," a novel attack where malicious content spreads between independent AI agents through shared persistent artifacts like documents. The core method involves an attacker injecting harmful data into an artifact, which is then stored, reproduced, and passed to subsequent agents, effectively creating a self-propagating "virus." The contribution is demonstrating this memory-hopping attack's feasibility and potential for widespread propagation across interconnected AI assistants.
items.figure_caption: Overview of our artifact-mediated propagation across independent assistants. A poisoned artifact infects an assistant’s memory ( hop 1 ). The assistant later reproduces the adversarial state into another artifact, which can infect a second assistant ( hop 2 ) and continue across further hops.

items.title: Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL
items.abstract: This paper introduces Retrospection-Only Fine-Tuning (ROFT), a novel method where language model agents improve by generating and learning from explanations of their own past actions, without external rewards or teachers. The core contribution is demonstrating that this "self-retrospection" alone, through next-token prediction on explanations, significantly enhances agent performance on complex tasks like software engineering.

Existing threat models assume attackers train models only with distillation, while a realistic distillation attack likely follows distillation with RL.

papers.title: FactorEngram: Factorized N-gram Memory with Basis-Level Gating for Language Models
papers.abstract: FactorEngram introduces a novel memory mechanism for language models that factorizes n-gram representations into shared basis vectors. This allows for more efficient parameter sharing and contextual gating at the basis level, enabling models to selectively retrieve relevant components of memory for polysemous patterns, unlike previous monolithic approaches. Its core contribution lies in enabling finer-grained memory access and improved semantic understanding through this factorized and gated memory structure.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of FactorEngram. Left: memory modules are residually inserted before the attention module at selected Transformer layers. Right: n-gram lookups retrieve coefficients that are concatenated and modulated by context-dependent basis-level gates. The shared dictionary participates in both gating and memory reconstruction. The reconstructed memory is projected, refined by a short causal convolution, and added to the backbone hidden state.

papers.title: Failure-Transparent Agents: Benchmarking Post-Failure Reporting in Tool-Using Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Failure-Transparent Agents (FTA), a benchmark designed to isolate and evaluate how tool-using language models report failures. FTA controls for external factors, allowing direct auditing of post-failure claims by fixing the observed failure and required evidence. The contribution lies in providing a controlled environment to measure and improve models' honesty and accuracy in reporting tool failures, leading to significant reductions in false success and fabricated details.
papers.figure_caption: FTA under a fixed post-failure evidence state. (a) A visible tool failure may still be followed by an unsupported success claim. (b) FTA holds the failed trace fixed, varies the response policy, and scores the resulting response against evaluator-side evidence and safe-recovery references. (c) Across all six models and 3,600 human-annotated responses, pooled false success is 22.8% under baseline, 9.3% with transparency, and 0.8% with the evidence contract.

papers.title: MechBench: Can AI Scientific Agents Discover Mechanisms Beyond Phenomenal Laws?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MechBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI scientific agents' ability to discover underlying mechanisms, not just observable laws. MechBench separates these capabilities by providing agents with observational data and context, then testing their understanding of internal scientific consequences through "mechanism probes." The benchmark's novel tasks are generated by mutating known mechanisms, pushing agents beyond memorization to true mechanistic discovery.
papers.figure_caption: From phenomenal-law recovery to mechanistic discovery.

papers.title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether different reasoning methods in LLMs share a common underlying mechanism. By training and comparing various models on a multi-hop reasoning task, they discover that models performing reasoning in latent space generalize better to out-of-distribution problems than those relying on explicit intermediate traces like Chain-of-Thought. Their key contribution is identifying a recurrent search algorithm in latent reasoning that enables this improved depth generalization.

papers.title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science
papers.abstract: This paper introduces AI Night-Scientist, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance LLM creativity in scientific ideation. It trains models to balance predictable "day science" with serendipitous "night science" by modeling creativity across action, process, and outcome. The core contribution is a method to generate more diverse and novel scientific proposals by teaching LLMs when and how to deviate from standard reasoning.
papers.figure_caption: Given an input task, creativity can be injected into three different axes of reasoning: action, process , and outcome . Moreover, each level can be executed with varying degrees of creativity .

papers.title: Representation Alignment as a Bottleneck in LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
papers.abstract: This paper argues that the failure of LLMs in chemical retrosynthesis planning stems from forcing them to simultaneously handle chemical analysis and planning language structuring. Their core method decomposes retrosynthesis into distinct stages: molecule mapping, reaction mapping, and PDDL generation. This approach successfully overcomes the bottleneck, demonstrating that representation alignment, not model capacity, is the key challenge, and highlighting the need for representation-centric design in future AI systems.

papers.title: RSI-Master: Structuring Experiments to Guide Autonomous Model Improvement
papers.abstract: RSI-Master introduces a novel framework for autonomous AI model improvement by structuring experiments to prevent "hacking" and "strategy lock-in." It employs an "Experiment OS" for regularized actions and traceable records, alongside a "Reviewer-Guided Research Orchestration" system that dynamically organizes exploration through a research Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). This approach ensures both safe, focused experimentation and broad exploration of research directions.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of RSI-Master . The Experiment OS defines permitted operations for data development, training, and evaluation and maintains persistent, linked experimental records. Reviewer-Guided Research Orchestration grows a DAG of research directions: Workers explore directions through experiments, Reviewers compare the resulting evidence, and the Main Agent uses their reviews to continue, verify, branch, or revise directions.

papers.title: Share-Borne AI Virus: Memory-Hopping Attacks Across LLM Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "artifact-mediated propagation," a novel attack where malicious content spreads between independent AI agents through shared persistent artifacts like documents. The core method involves an attacker injecting harmful data into an artifact, which is then stored, reproduced, and passed to subsequent agents, effectively creating a self-propagating "virus." The contribution is demonstrating this memory-hopping attack's feasibility and potential for widespread propagation across interconnected AI assistants.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of our artifact-mediated propagation across independent assistants. A poisoned artifact infects an assistant’s memory ( hop 1 ). The assistant later reproduces the adversarial state into another artifact, which can infect a second assistant ( hop 2 ) and continue across further hops.

papers.title: Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Retrospection-Only Fine-Tuning (ROFT), a novel method where language model agents improve by generating and learning from explanations of their own past actions, without external rewards or teachers. The core contribution is demonstrating that this "self-retrospection" alone, through next-token prediction on explanations, significantly enhances agent performance on complex tasks like software engineering.
